question:
How to ergonomically perform matrix multiplication inside Polars streaming engine?

I have a large table of data, in the range of hundreds of millions of rows/events, each which has around 50 numerical columns, call them c1 through c50. For each event, say I want to perform matrix-vector multiplication where I define a matrix via, e.g. M = ( (c1, c2, c3), (c4, c5, c6), (c7, c8, c9) ) and a vector via, e.g. v = (c48, c49, c50) Now, I could do this via numpy, but due to the size of my dataset, a single operation exceeds RAM, an increasingly important consideration these days. The obvious solution is to split the job into batches and manually adjust the size of each. However, it's not a fun task, and I have discovered the Polars library can do the job by using the streaming engine, and saving the following outputs: v1 = c1 * c48 + c2 * c49 + c3 * c50 and similarly for the other two outputs vector components. Notably, using the streaming engine means I don't have to thinking about partitioning the dataset into batches. Thankfully, all these operations being only per-row means all the multiplication and addition are available in the streaming engine. However, if I have to chain matrix multiplications together, or the matrices get larger, you can imagine just how cumbersome this gets. Thus, I'm trying to think through a system or wrapper to automate the expansion of all the linear algebra operations into multiplication and addition, but I haven't had much luck, though it probably shouldn't be a very hard problem. I know polars might not have been designed for this specifically, but its streaming engine makes this direction very appealing compared to numpy. Thank
llm_attempt:
Since every entry of a matrix-vector or matrix-matrix product is just a sum of column products, you don't need real linear algebra support in Polars: generate the sum-of-products expressions programmatically and let the streaming engine treat them like any other expression. Represent M as a nested list of column-name strings and v as a list of column names, then build one expression per output using pl.sum_horizontal:

def matvec(M, v, out_names):
    return [pl.sum_horizontal([pl.col(M[i][j]) * pl.col(v[j]) for j in range(len(v))]).alias(out_names[i]) for i in range(len(M))]

lf.with_columns(matvec(M, v, ["v1","v2","v3"]))

This is pure Python building an expression list, so it composes fine with lazy/streaming execution. For chained multiplications, feed one stage's output column names in as the next stage's v, or symbolically multiply two nested lists of expressions before calling with_columns once. Wrap this in a small helper keyed by matrix shape and you get automatic expansion without ever materializing more than the streaming engine already batches.

question:
Why is Airflow Bash operator not passing XCom to another operator?

I'm working on a task group that needs to pass a variable from a BashOperator to another BashOperator . Each bash operator is invoking Python, and the first Python script needs to return a string in a variable that the second bash operator will take and continue with: first_status = BashOperator( task_id=1st_taskid_str, bash_command=f"python myscript.py --dag_id '{dag.dag_id}' \ --task_id '{1st_taskid_str}' --dag_conf configuration_string", retries=10, dag=dag, retry_delay=timedelta(minutes=1), do_xcom_push=True, ) #step 2 second_status = BashOperator( task_id=process_file_task_id ,bash_command=f"python secondscript.py --dag_id '{dag.dag_id}' \ --task_id '{2nd_task_id}' --dag_conf configuration_string --file '{{ ti.xcom_pull(task_ids=\"{1st_taskid_str}\") }}'" ,dag=dag ) first_status >> second_status When I view the XCom from the first_status task , I'm not seeing the variable that is logged by the Python script invoked. How can I get this variable passed from the first bash operator to the second bash operator?
reference_answer: BashOperator with do_xcom_push=True only stores the last line of stdout in XCom. So in myscript.py , make sure the very last line just prints the value you want: print("/tmp/output.csv") Then pull it in the next task like you did: --file '{{ ti.xcom_pull(task_ids="first_task") }}' That will pass the variable correctly.
llm_attempt: BashOperator's do_xcom_push only captures the single last line written to the command's stdout; that exact string becomes the XCom value, nothing else. Check: (1) myscript.py must end with a bare print(value), not logging (which usually goes to stderr and isn't captured), as the very last thing it outputs, any later print/debug/warning line or trailing blank line will overwrite or blank out what gets pushed; (2) the task must exit 0 for XCom to be recorded; (3) run the exact bash_command manually and confirm the last stdout line is exactly what you expect. Also verify the f-string in your bash_command isn't mangling anything unexpected. Then inspect Admin > XComs in the Airflow UI for that specific first_status task instance to see the literal value stored; if it's empty or None, the problem is entirely in what myscript.py prints to stdout, not in how the second BashOperator's Jinja template pulls it.

question:
Not all files have gcno with bazel --coverage

NB I have the custom targets which run by python scripts. So I couldn't use bazel coverage directly for this one. 1. I defined in .bazelrc build:coverage --collect_code_coverage build:coverage --instrumentation_filter="^//src[/:]" coverage --instrumentation_filter="^//src[/:]" In the root BUILD config_setting( name = "Coverage", flag_values = { ":coverage": "true", }, ) bool_flag( name = "coverage", build_setting_default = False, ) In the cc_binary wrapper I use + select({"//:Coverage": coverageCopts, "//conditions:default": [], }), // and select({"//:Coverage": coverageLopts, "//conditions:default": [], }), where coverageCopts = ["--coverage", "-fprofile-abs-path", "-fprofile-arcs", "-ftest-coverage"] coverageLopts = ["--coverage", "-lgcov"] and run this python script (from bazel) like this: bazel run --subcommands --//\:coverage=true script:runner But for some mystical reasons I have a lack of gcno files. although there are these gcno 's for neighboring files from the same library. Grepping for bazel --subcommands indicates the presences of --coverage flag for this cpp file. I did bazel clean --expunge - same result.
llm_attempt: Two likely causes. First, your custom coverage bool_flag and Bazel's native collect_code_coverage/instrumentation_filter are independent mechanisms; your select() only adds -fprofile-arcs/-ftest-coverage compiler flags to targets that explicitly use your wrapper macro. If any cc_library in the dependency chain doesn't route through that same wrapper, its objects compile without --coverage and produce no gcno, even though sibling files in a library that does use the wrapper get instrumented. Audit every cc_library/cc_binary between your binary and the file missing gcno to confirm all of them apply the wrapper's copts/linkopts. Second, instrumentation_filter="^//src[/:]" matches by target label/package; files living in a different package, an external repo, or generated under bazel-out won't be instrumented by Bazel's native bookkeeping regardless of your manual copts. Check the exact label of the affected files against that regex. bazel query 'deps(//your:binary)' --output=label_kind, cross-checked against each target's copts, is the fastest way to find the target missing the wrapper.

question:
GreatExpectations; ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing; '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timedelta' and 'int'

I try to load many different csv files and data check them with GreatExpecatations. It works for ExpectColumnValuesToNotBeNull, ExpectColumnValuesToBeUnique and ExpectColumnValuesToMatchRegex. But with ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing I get an error that I am trying to solve for the last 4 hours unsuccessfully. To reproduce on a small scale, create 'Test Calendar.csv': Date 1995-01-03 1995-01-04 1995-01-05 The python script is: # %% import great_expectations as gx import pandas as pd # %% # Get the Ephemeral Data Context context = gx.get_context() assert type(context).__name__ == "EphemeralDataContext" # %% context = gx.get_context() # %% df = pd.read_csv("Test Calendar.csv", parse_dates=["Date"]) # %% pd.to_datetime(df["Date"]) # %% data_source = context.data_sources.add_pandas("pandas") data_asset = data_source.add_dataframe_asset(name="pd dataframe asset") batch_definition = data_asset.add_batch_definition_whole_dataframe("batch definition") batch = batch_definition.get_batch(batch_parameters={"dataframe": df}) # %% # Create an Expectation Suite suite = gx.ExpectationSuite(name="expectation_suite") # %% suite.add_expectation( gx.expectations.ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing(column="Date") ) # %% validation_results = batch.validate(suite) print(validation_results) The script itself runs without error, but yields amongst others raise gx_exceptions.MetricResolutionError(\ngreat_expectations.exceptions.exceptions.MetricResolutionError: '>=' not supported between instances of 'Timedelta' and 'int'\n", "exception_message": "'>=' not supported between instances of 'Timedelta' a
reference_answer: ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing looks like it wants a numeric type. Or at least a type that it can compare against a default value of 0 . You did a good job of converting .to_datetime(), and usually that's exactly what we want. But here, prefer to work with "seconds since epoch". (Well, OK, nanoseconds.) df['Date'] = df.Date.astype('int64') That will give us a nice "success": true result. Please consider reporting a bug against the upstream vendor , and leave the BugID in a comment here. The docs promise that this expectation ... works for numeric or datetime data.
llm_attempt: This is a known limitation of ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing (and Decreasing) against datetime64 columns in current Great Expectations: internally the metric computes successive differences, which come back as pandas Timedelta, and compares them against a plain int threshold (0), causing the ">=" not supported between Timedelta and int error. It works for null/unique/regex expectations because those don't do numeric or temporal comparisons. Workaround: don't validate the raw datetime column directly; convert it to an integer representation first, e.g. df["Date"] = df["Date"].astype("int64") for nanosecond timestamps, or map to ordinal via pd.Timestamp.toordinal, and run ExpectColumnValuesToBeIncreasing against that numeric column instead. Also check the Great Expectations GitHub issues for this expectation plus datetime columns; it has been reported before, so upgrading or downgrading your great_expectations version may already resolve it. If you need to keep the original Date column for other checks, just add the int-cast version as an extra column in the same dataframe purely for this one expectation.

question:
TexStudio macro running python script but writing return string in message box

I make my drawings in Krita while I write my report in TexStudio. In Krita I select part of the drawing and put it on the clipboard. I put my cursor in the .tex file at the desired position and run the macro. The macro takes the current file name and passes it to a python script. The latter converts the clipboard content and saves it in a .png file (not in the python script I added below). The png file name is added to a string starting with \includegraphics ... . The latter string is returned by the python script to the macro. The macro should insert this TeX command string at the cursor position in the current .tex document. The editor.insertText command DOES NOT insert the text in the open current .tex document where the macro is triggered but it writes the command in the "Messages" box. I added also the command for showing the return string from the Python script in an "alert" but this opens the alert box without content. My simplified python script follows below: #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os import sys def main(fn): print(repr(str(fn)+"xxxx"),end="") if __name__ == "__main__": main("Hello World") The macro code is the following: var proc = system("/home/stefan/ARCHIVE/SCRIPTS/latex_automation/main.py"); proc.waitForFinished(); var output = proc.standardOutput; // Ensure the editor is focused app.focusEditor(); // Confirm editor is valid and insert if (editor) { editor.insertText(output); } else { QMessageBox.information(null, "Error", "No active .tex document found."); } alert(output)
llm_attempt: A couple of likely issues. First, in TexStudio's scripting API editor is a function, not a property; you need editor().insertText(output), not editor.insertText(output). Using it without calling it can silently target the wrong place, consistent with your output landing in the Messages panel instead of the document. Second, proc.standardOutput may need explicit string conversion in your Qt/TexStudio version; try var output = ""+proc.standardOutput, or read via proc.readAllStandardOutput() depending on version. Third, clean up what Python prints: repr(str(fn)+"xxxx") wraps the string in quotes and escape characters, which is almost certainly not the literal includegraphics text you want inserted; print the raw string with print(result, end="") (no repr, no trailing newline) so output is exactly the text to insert. Test incrementally: alert(typeof output) and alert(output.length) first, to confirm the process actually returned something before troubleshooting insertText's target further.

question:
Numpy importing error in mod_wsgi app on Fedora 43

I'm getting an error when importing numpy from an Apache mod_wsgi application on Fedora 43 and 42. It does not happen in Rocky Linux 9, the production server. app.wsgi: import sys sys.path.insert(0, '/var/www/html/test/') from test import application test.py: import numpy def application(environ, start_response): status = '200 OK' output = b'Hello World!' response_headers = [('Content-type', 'text/plain'), ('Content-Length', str(len(output)))] start_response(status, response_headers) return [output] Error log: mod_wsgi (pid=187553): Failed to exec Python script file '/var/www/html/test/app.wsgi'. mod_wsgi (pid=187553): Exception occurred processing WSGI script '/var/www/html/test/app.wsgi'. Traceback (most recent call last): File "/var/www/html/test/venv/lib64/python3.14/site-packages/numpy/_core/__init__.py", line 22, in <module> from . import multiarray File "/var/www/html/test/venv/lib64/python3.14/site-packages/numpy/_core/multiarray.py", line 11, in <module> from . import _multiarray_umath, overrides ImportError: /var/www/html/test/venv/lib64/python3.14/site-packages/numpy/_core/_multiarray_umath.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so: failed to map segment from shared object The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception: Traceback (most recent call last): File "/var/www/html/test/venv/lib64/python3.14/site-packages/numpy/__init__.py", line 112, in <module> from numpy.__config__ import show_config File "/var/www/html/test/venv/lib64/python3.14/site-packages/numpy/__config__.py", line 4, in <module> from numpy._core._multiarray_umath import ( ...<3 lines>
llm_attempt: "failed to map segment from shared object" when loading a compiled .so under mod_wsgi on Fedora is the classic signature of SELinux blocking execmem/execmod for a shared library mmap'd by httpd. Fedora ships SELinux enforcing by default; Rocky 9's policy or your venv's file contexts apparently allow it while Fedora 42/43 don't, often because the venv was created or copied in a way that left it with the wrong context (e.g. user_tmp_t) instead of one httpd is allowed to execute from. Check sudo ausearch -m avc -ts recent (or journalctl) for AVC denials around the time of the request; denials referencing httpd_t plus execmem/execmod confirm this. Fixes: relabel the venv with sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html/test/venv after ensuring the parent directory has a correct context, or more broadly sudo setsebool -P httpd_execmem 1. Also confirm the filesystem isn't mounted noexec. This is unrelated to your numpy version; any compiled extension loaded by mod_wsgi can trigger it.

question:
KeyError: 'Cache only has 0 layers, attempted to access layer with index 0'

raise KeyError(f"Cache only has {len(self)} layers, attempted to access layer with index {layer_idx}") KeyError: 'Cache only has 0 layers, attempted to access layer with index 0' When I try to run train_RAMLLaMA in RAMQA, I encounter this problem. When I read other posts about this problem, they said to change the transformer version to 4.35.0 . But for this model, I also need transform.gamma2 for the unsloth package. The transfromar.gamma2 only exist in >= 4.43.0 torch 2.3.0 transformers 4.44.2 unsloth 2024.8
reference_answer: This error is almost always a KV-cache mismatch, (the Cache object introduced in recent versions). In training, you don’t need the KV cache at all. model.config.use_cache = False
llm_attempt: This looks like a mismatch between the model's custom KV-cache handling code and the transformers version's Cache API, not a hyperparameter bug. Since transformers introduced Cache objects (e.g. DynamicCache) to replace the old tuple-of-tuples past_key_values, that cache starts empty until something calls cache.update(...); code written for the legacy format that indexes past_key_values[0] directly will hit exactly this "Cache only has 0 layers" error if nothing has populated layer 0, likely if RAMLLaMA's custom modeling code predates the Cache API changes between versions 4.35 and 4.44. Since you need >=4.43 for gamma2 but the RAMLLaMA/unsloth modeling code may not be updated for the newer Cache internals, the two requirements may genuinely conflict in your current combination. Check the RAMQA/unsloth repo's issues or changelog for a transformers version known to support gamma2 without this break, or patch the custom attention code to initialize past_key_values = DynamicCache() and call .update() instead of indexing it positionally. This likely needs an upstream code fix rather than a config change.

question:
Python win32com Outlook.Application fails with “Server execution failed”

I’m trying to automate sending an email via Outlook from Python using win32com.client , but Outlook COM fails to start with “Server execution failed / Operation unavailable” . The error occurs before any email object is created , so it’s not related to recipients, attachments, or message content. Environment Windows 11 Python 3.14 pywin32 installed Microsoft Outlook installed (New Outlook UI enabled; classic Outlook may also be present) What I’ve already tried Running the script from a .py file (not Jupyter / notebook) Opening Outlook manually before running the script Killing all OUTLOOK.EXE processes and retrying Using both Dispatch and DispatchEx Calling pythoncom.CoInitialize() Questions Is Python 3.14 compatible with pywin32 and Outlook COM automation? Does the New Outlook app prevent Outlook.Application COM automation even if classic Outlook is installed? Is this a known limitation or environment issue with recent Python versions? Any guidance on whether this is a Python version issue, Outlook version issue, or a Windows/COM limitation would be appreciated.
reference_answer: You must make sure the old desktop Outlook is installed and works properly. The new Outlook is JS based and exposes no externally accessible API. Very likely this error is due to a mismatch between the security contexts. Outlook is a singleton, so win32com.client will connect to the running instance of Outlook if it is available. COM system refuses to marshal calls between processes with different security contexts. Make sure Outlook is not running when your code runs or make sure both processes run in the same security context. Also make sure your Python code is running under the identity of the current Windows user.
llm_attempt: This is almost certainly the New Outlook, not Python 3.14 or pywin32. New Outlook is a rebuilt web-based client and does not implement the classic COM Automation server (Outlook.Application) the way desktop Outlook does; even with classic Outlook also installed, if New Outlook is the active one, COM activation can fail with exactly "Server execution failed" because the registered server behavior differs between the two. Fix: turn off "Try the New Outlook" (toggle in the top-right of Outlook) so classic Outlook is what's actually running, open it manually once, then retry win32com.client.Dispatch("Outlook.Application"). Also make sure your Python process and Outlook run at the same privilege/integrity level and in the same user session; COM activation commonly fails across an elevation or session boundary (e.g. script run as admin, Outlook run as normal user). Python 3.14 plus pywin32 isn't a known blocker for Outlook automation by itself, as long as pywin32 finished installing cleanly (rerun its post-install script if unsure).

question:
Bundling Jinja2 temlate with UV

I am trying to include jinja2 templates within my uv build but it does not seem to work. My directory structure is as follows. project/ ├── src/ │ ├── mypackage/ │ └──── j2/ (all templates live here) └── pyproject.toml Following is my py project toml [project] name = "dojipipeline" version = "0.1.0" description = "Add your description here" readme = "README.md" requires-python = ">=3.12" dependencies = [ "groq>=0.16.0", "jinja2>=3.1.5", "pydantic>=2.10.6", "python-dotenv>=1.0.1", "pyyaml>=6.0.2", ] My work around is to capture all the j2 as doc_string in .py file like below and import it #j2_template.py GENERATE_DATA_MODEL = """ You are a data governance expert and are tasked to perform the following { % for task in tasks % } {{ task }} { % endfor % } =========================== {% if contexts %} Following are the contexts for the tasks: {% for context in contexts %} {{ context }} {% endfor %} {% endif %} The required responses must be in JSON format. "response": { "data": {{ data_shema }} "thoughts": List of thoughts } Generate a valid data object and explain your thought process. Answer only with json and do not include any other information. """
llm_attempt:
Most likely cause: your build backend (hatchling, uv's default) determines included files from your VCS file list by default; if the j2 templates under src/mypackage/j2/ aren't tracked by git, they get silently excluded from the built wheel even though they exist on disk. Run git add on the template files first and check git status. If they're tracked and still missing, add an explicit include:

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/mypackage"]

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]
"src/mypackage/j2" = "mypackage/j2"

or add [tool.hatch.build] include = ["src/mypackage/j2/**"]. Separately, don't rely on relative filesystem paths to find templates at runtime since that breaks once installed as a wheel; use importlib.resources instead: importlib.resources.files("mypackage.j2").joinpath("template.j2").read_text(), or point Jinja2's PackageLoader("mypackage", "j2") at it, which is built exactly for this and works both from source checkouts and installed wheels.

question:
Why do AWS Lambdas created from a non-Amazon image fail to return a dictionary?

I have an image c created by AWS Imagebuilder that uses debian:bookworm-slim as the base, and then runs apt install -y --no-install-suggests texlive-latex-extra python3.11 python3-pip && pip3 install --break-system-packages awslambdaric . In the main file, among other things, I call event.get("queryStringParameters", event)["key"] . If I call c from the "Test" tab in the AWS console, the function succeeds as expected; however, if I call it from the function URL in my browser (ie, .../?key=123&... ), I get an 502 - "Internal Server Error" message. Looking at Cloudwatch tells me that the error is with the ...["key"] call, as it results in a KeyError . However, it seems that this log is not related to 502 error I received --- if I add a print line under the supposedly erroneous [] call, the function returns the string. This seems to be because I am returning a dictionary as a payload (ie, {"statusCode":..., "headers":..., "body":...} , as described here: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/python-handler.html#python-handler-return ) --- if I modify the function to return anything else, like a string or a list, the function is able to execute successfully. I can not replicate this with another Lambda that uses the default AWS Python base image (ie, a code editor window appears in the "Image" tab) --- while the same line appears in the error log, the function is able to return the dictionary successfully. Why does this only happen with non-Amazon images?
reference_answer: The dict[key] operation fails because event.get("queryStringParameters", event) returns None when the Lambda is called via a Function URL without query parameters. Accessing ["key"] on None raises a TypeError . This isn’t caused by the non-Amazon image, but by differences in the event format between Function URL and console test. Use this safer code to fix: value = (event.get("queryStringParameters") or {}).get("key") This avoids errors when queryStringParameters is None .
llm_attempt: This smells like a version difference in awslambdaric (the Lambda Runtime Interface Client) between AWS's own Python base images and whatever pip installs on plain Debian. AWS's managed images bundle a build with mature Function-URL response handling, correctly detecting the payload-format-2.0 shape (statusCode/headers/body/isBase64Encoded) and serializing it into an HTTP response, while an independently pip-installed awslambdaric can lag behind or handle that path differently, consistent with the console "Test" invoke (which just echoes any return value as raw JSON) succeeding while only the HTTP function-URL path fails on a dict return. Compare pip show awslambdaric's version against what AWS's base image ships, and try pinning to the latest release. Also double check your returned dict's keys and types exactly match {"statusCode": int, "headers": {...}, "body": str, "isBase64Encoded": bool}; function URLs are stricter about this than the Test tab. If pinning doesn't help, this is worth filing against the aws-lambda-python-runtime-interface-client repo directly.

question:
How to convert matrix to block matrix using Numpy

Say I have a matrix like Matrix = [[A11, A12, A13, A14], [A21, A22, A23, A24], [A31, A32, A33, A34], [A41, A42, A43, A44]] , and suppose I want to convert it to a block matrix [[A,B], [C,D]] , where A = [[A11, A12], [A21, A22]] B = [[A13, A14], [A23, A24]] C = [[A31, A32], [A41, A42]] D = [[A33, A34], [A43, A44]] . What do I need to type to quickly extract the matrices A, B, C, and D?
reference_answer: Without using loops, you can reshape your array (and reorder the dimensions with moveaxis ): A, B, C, D = np.moveaxis(Matrix.reshape((2,2,2,2)), 1, 2).reshape(-1, 2, 2) Or: (A, B), (C, D) = np.moveaxis(Matrix.reshape((2,2,2,2)), 1, 2) For a generic answer on an arbitrary shape: x, y = Matrix.shape (A, B), (C, D) = np.moveaxis(Matrix.reshape((2, x//2, 2, y//2)), 1, 2) Output: # A array([['A11', 'A12'], ['A21', 'A22']], dtype='<U3') # B array([['A13', 'A14'], ['A23', 'A24']], dtype='<U3') # C array([['A31', 'A32'], ['A41', 'A42']], dtype='<U3') # D array([['A33', 'A34'], ['A43', 'A44']], dtype='<U3')
llm_attempt:
If Matrix is a numpy array (wrap nested lists with np.array(Matrix) first), just slice it into quadrants:

import numpy as np
M = np.array(Matrix)
A = M[:2, :2]
B = M[:2, 2:]
C = M[2:, :2]
D = M[2:, 2:]

For splitting an n by n array into equal b by b blocks in general, reshape plus swapaxes does it in one shot:

n, b = M.shape[0], 2
blocks = M.reshape(n//b, b, n//b, b).swapaxes(1, 2)
# blocks[0,0]==A, blocks[0,1]==B, blocks[1,0]==C, blocks[1,1]==D

Or use np.split twice if you'd rather avoid reshape/swapaxes:

top, bottom = np.vsplit(M, 2)
A, B = np.hsplit(top, 2)
C, D = np.hsplit(bottom, 2)

Any of these work; direct slicing is simplest for one fixed known layout, reshape/swapaxes is nicer when you want all blocks generated programmatically for an arbitrary block size.

question:
pandas version 2.1.4 method mad()

I looked in the documentation for version 2.1.4 and didn't find anything about Mean Absolute Deviation, which in previous versions was mad(). Can anyone tell me which method in the current version works like mad()?
reference_answer: mad() method has been deprecated, however, you can still calculate the MAD manually using simple formula with the mean() method and absolute differences. Here's the code. import pandas as pd s = pd.Series([2, 3, 5, 7, 11]) # Compute MAD manually mad = (s - s.mean()).abs().mean() print(mad) I hope this will help you a little.
llm_attempt:
DataFrame.mad() and Series.mad() were deprecated in pandas 1.5 and removed in 2.0, so there's no direct replacement method in 2.1.4; pandas' own deprecation notice recommends computing it manually instead:

(df - df.mean()).abs().mean()

for a DataFrame column-wise, or for a Series:

(s - s.mean()).abs().mean()

If you actually want median absolute deviation rather than mean absolute deviation, use scipy: from scipy.stats import median_abs_deviation, then median_abs_deviation(df, axis=0); or in pandas terms, (df - df.median()).abs().median(). There's no plan to reintroduce mad() as a method, so the manual one-liner is the officially suggested replacement rather than a workaround, and it's safe to rely on going forward.

question:
How to download protected PDF (ViewDocument) using Selenium or requests?

I'm trying to download a protected PDF from the New York State Courts NYSCEF website using Python. question:
Can label or button act as parent in tkinter?

I always thought that only frame and other container elements can be parent, but recently when I tried the below code, it seemed to work perfectly without any error. import os import tkinter as tk from PIL import Image, ImageTk BASE_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)) main = tk.Tk() main.title("Main Window") main.config(bg="#E4E2E2") main.geometry("700x400") frame = tk.Frame(master=main) frame.config(bg="#d1c9c9") frame.pack() label2 = tk.Label(master=frame, text="Password") label2.config(bg="#d1c9c9", fg="#000") label2.pack(side=tk.TOP) button = tk.Button(master=frame, text="Submit") button.config(bg="#161515", fg="#ffffff") button.pack(side=tk.TOP) entry1 = tk.Entry(master=button) entry1.config(bg="#fff", fg="#000") entry1.pack(side=tk.TOP) main.mainloop() The entry seems to be appearing inside the button when i try it on my linux PC. So, is it fine to use labels, button widgets and others as parents? Will it cause any issues on other OS?
reference_answer: Any widget can be the parent of another widget. While unusual, it's perfectly acceptable to make a label or a button a parent of another widget. This might not always work the way you expect though, since some widgets have interactive behaviors that won't account for child widgets. For example, if you add another button as a child of a button, either the parent or child button may not work the way you expect when you click on it. I advise not using buttons as a parent. There are usually better ways to solve whatever problem you are trying to solve.
llm_attempt: Technically yes; in Tkinter the master argument just needs to be any Tk widget, since every widget is backed by an actual window internally, and pack/grid/place only require a valid Tk window to attach children to. Tkinter doesn't restrict parenthood to Frame/Toplevel/Canvas at the C level; that's a convention, not an enforced rule. It's unsupported in practice, though: Label and Button aren't designed to manage child geometry, so results are inconsistent across platforms. You're seeing the Entry render inside the Button on Linux, but on Windows or macOS, which use more strictly themed widget rendering especially with ttk, the same code can clip children, ignore them, size oddly, or look broken, because those widgets don't reserve or manage internal layout space the way a Frame does. Stick to Frame, LabelFrame, Canvas, or Toplevel as containers for anything meant to hold child widgets, and treat this working on your Linux setup as non-portable rather than as confirmation it's a supported pattern.

question:

My intention is to create a charuco board object, which supports custom ids. Here is the code snippet being used. def __init__(self, squaresX=11, squaresY=8, squareLength=0.015, markerLength=0.011, dict=cv2.aruco.DICT_5X5_250, start_id=0): self.squaresX = squaresX self.squaresY = squaresY self.squareLength = squareLength self.markerLength = markerLength self.aruco_dict = cv2.aruco.getPredefinedDictionary(dict) self.start_id = start_id num_markers_x = squaresX - 1 num_markers_y = squaresY - 1 num_markers = num_markers_x * num_markers_y if start_id + num_markers > self.aruco_dict.bytesList.shape[0]: raise ValueError(f"Not enough markers in dictionary for board (required: {num_markers})") marker_ids = np.arange(start_id, start_id + num_markers, dtype=np.int32).reshape(num_markers_y, num_markers_x) self.board = cv2.aruco.CharucoBoard( (self.squaresX, self.squaresY), self.squareLength, self.markerLength, self.aruco_dict, marker_ids ) However when I create self.board , there is a segmentation error (keep in mind when I'm creating the object, I'm using the same arguments as the default arguments to the __init__ method. cv2.__version__ returns 4.11.0
reference_answer: The problem seems to be: You are providing way too many marker_ids . ChArUco uses one marker per white chessboard square , as is also mentioned in its OpenCV documentation : ChArUco board is a planar chessboard where the markers are placed inside the white squares of a chessboard. The pattern you currently seem to employ is: one ID per square corner inside the board (as a 2-d array). The pattern you actually need is: exactly as many marker_ids as there are white squares in the chessboard of the given square count (as a 1-d array). This is reflected by the integer division, which will produce the same result as a regular division in this case. For odd-numbered square counts (i.e. with both squaresX and squa
llm_attempt:
The likely bug is your marker-count formula, not custom ids per se. A ChArUco board places markers only on alternating squares of the checkerboard, so the correct marker count for a squaresX by squaresY board is (squaresX*squaresY)//2, not (squaresX-1)*(squaresY-1) as you compute; for 11x8 that's 44 versus your 70. Passing an ids array of the wrong length, reshaped into a 2D grid on top of that, means OpenCV's C++ CharucoBoard constructor reads or writes past the bounds of the array it's given internally, a textbook segfault cause rather than something Python would catch as an exception. Fix: compute num_markers = (self.squaresX * self.squaresY) // 2, and pass a flat 1D array with no reshape:

marker_ids = np.arange(start_id, start_id + num_markers, dtype=np.int32)

Pass that 1D array directly as the ids argument. Also cross-check against the cv2.aruco documentation or examples for your exact 4.11.0 build, since the expected marker count and layout convention can vary slightly by board/marker variant.

question:
Can someone help explain Python's mypy issue with Incompatible return value type due to covariance when returning a sub type of a union

Apologies if there is a straightforward answer already that I'm too smooth brained to see. I am working with Python 3.13+ and Mypy 1.19.1. I've read mypy's docs, read several similar questions/answers here, and spent hours with AI. I'm trying to write a JSON decoder in python using functional programming that returns a generic Result rather than raise errors. I believe the issue is due to mypy thinking the underlying data structure can at some point change in the future, and using 'covariant' fixes the issue, but mypy complains about covariant's being parameters. Can someone look at the following code and mypy error and explain why it's happening, as simply as possible, and how I could change the code to resolve the errors while retaining immutable dataclasses? from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Literal @dataclass(frozen=True) class Ok[T]: value: T @dataclass(frozen=True) class Err[E]: value: E type Result[T, E] = Ok[T] | Err[E] @dataclass(frozen=True) class Dog: nm: str kind: Literal['Dog'] = 'Dog' @dataclass(frozen=True) class Cat: nm: str kind: Literal['Cat'] = 'Cat' type Animal = Dog | Cat def decodeDog(slop: dict) -> Result[Dog, str]: try: return Ok(Dog(slop["nm"])) except Exception as e: return Err(f"Decode Error: {e}") def decodeCat(slop: dict) -> Result[Cat, str]: try: return Ok(Cat(slop["nm"])) except Exception as e: return Err(f"Decode Error: {e}") def decodeAnimal(slop: dict) -> Result[Animal, str]: match slop.get("kind"): case "Dog": return decodeDog(slop) case "Cat": return decodeCat(slop) case _: return Err("Unknown Animal") if __name__ == "_
llm_attempt: mypy treats user-defined generic classes as invariant in their type parameters by default. Ok[Dog] is therefore not assignable to Ok[Animal] even though Dog is one arm of the Animal union; invariance means the type argument must match exactly, not merely be compatible. Marking T covariant would fix the return-type check, but your frozen dataclass still generates __init__(self, value: T), a parameter position, and mypy forbids a covariant TypeVar from appearing in any parameter position, even a synthesized one, because covariance is only sound when T appears solely in output positions. That's the contradiction: the type is read-only in spirit, but the generated constructor makes it look mutable to the checker. Practical fixes: narrow at each call site with an explicit cast, return cast(Result[Animal, str], decodeDog(slop)); or add a targeted type: ignore[return-value] comment on each delegating return; or avoid delegating directly and instead pattern-match the inner Ok/Err and rewrap it, e.g. match decodeDog(slop): case Ok(v): return Ok(v), case Err(e): return Err(e), which mypy accepts because Dog is directly assignable to Animal there.

question:
Transforming TypeVarTuple in Python

In Python I can use the TypeVarTuple to something generic like this: def foo[*Ts](generic_tuple: tuple[*Ts]) -> tuple[*Ts]: ... But what if I want to return a tuple where the types are not *Ts themselves, but some type involving it. For example list[*Ts] . Conceptually I want: def foo[*Ts](generic_tuple: tuple[*Ts]) -> tuple[list[T] for T in *Ts]: ... Is this possible? As far as I can see it isn't but I thought I'd check.
reference_answer: Of course as soon as I post the question I find the answer... There's an open issue from 2022 for exactly this feature. So it isn't possible.
llm_attempt: No, this isn't possible today. PEP 646's TypeVarTuple only lets you pass *Ts through unchanged, or prepend/append fixed items around it, like tuple[int, *Ts], or bind it to another TypeVarTuple; there's no elementwise "map" operation defined in the type system to transform each element of the tuple, such as wrapping each in list[...], while staying generic over arbitrary arity. Neither the PEP nor current mypy or pyright implement anything like the tuple[list[T] for T in *Ts] syntax you're picturing, and there's no separate PEP currently proposing it. Practical workarounds: if you only need a handful of fixed arities, write explicit overloads for each, one returning tuple[list[T1]], another tuple[list[T1], list[T2]], and so on; or give up precision and type it as tuple[list[Any], ...]; or, if the elements are actually homogeneous, use a plain TypeVar with a regular variadic tuple or Sequence instead of TypeVarTuple, since that case never needed per-element mapping in the first place.

question:
error raised from solve when using Q but not for q

I have an error with this code from sympy import * x,y = symbols('x y') Q=1 gf = x+y,5*x-y-Q k=solve(gf,'x','Q','y') File "C:\Users\mcaka\HydroD\stubborn.py", line 5, in <module> k=solve(gf,'X','x','b','Q') ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "C:\Users\mcaka\PycharmProjects\pythonProject\.venv\Lib\site-packages\sympy\solvers\solvers.py", line 1038, in solve f, symbols, swap_sym = recast_to_symbols(f, symbols) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "C:\Users\mcaka\PycharmProjects\pythonProject\.venv\Lib\site-packages\sympy\solvers\solvers.py", line 108, in recast_to_symbols new_f.append(isubs(swap_sym)) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "C:\Users\mcaka\PycharmProjects\pythonProject\.venv\Lib\site-packages\sympy\core\basic.py", line 1074, in subs sequence = [(sympify_old(s1), sympify_new(s2)) for s1, s2 in sequence] ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "C:\Users\mcaka\PycharmProjects\pythonProject\.venv\Lib\site-packages\sympy\core\basic.py", line 1065, in sympify_old return sympify(old, strict=True) ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "C:\Users\mcaka\PycharmProjects\pythonProject\.venv\Lib\site-packages\sympy\core\sympify.py", line 454, in sympify raise SympifyError(a) sympy.core.sympify.SympifyError: SympifyError: <sympy.assumptions.ask.AssumptionKeys object at 0x00000203F7F279E0> When I change Q to q then no error is raised. x,y = symbols('x y') q=1 gf = x+y,5*x-y-q k=solve(gf,'x','q','y') Why does it depend on the case of the variable that I use?
reference_answer: It makes sense to understand what happens under the hood before you can understand why 'Q' causes that error. When you call solve with string arguments, it tries to replace the strings with symbols. One of the first attempts is to import all symbols from sympy.* and to replace string with these symbols. The string 'Q' is replaced with sympy.Q . There are no symbols in sympy.* for 'b' , 'c' or 'q' . In that case, solve creates new symbols for these strings. The call solve(gf,'x','c','b','Q') is similar to solve(gf,symbols('x'),symbols('c'),symbols('b'),Q) but Q can't be used in this context. It is an instance that is expected to be used with assumptions. The error is raised in https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/master/sympy/core/sympify.py#L480 in solve , because simpify doesn't know how to handle an instance of type sympy.assumptions.ask.AssumptionKeys .
llm_attempt: This is a name collision, not case-sensitivity in general. Q is a reserved name in sympy: sympy.Q is the assumptions query object (sympy.assumptions.ask.Q, used for things like Q.positive(x)), which lands in your namespace via from sympy import *. When you pass the string "Q" into solve(gf, "x", "Q", "y"), sympy has to sympify that string, and it resolves against sympy's own globals first; it finds the existing Q assumptions object instead of creating or matching an ordinary Symbol, so recast_to_symbols fails trying to sympify that AssumptionKeys object as though it were a plain symbol name, raising SympifyError. Lowercase "q" has no such collision, so it works fine. Fix: avoid the capital letter Q, renaming your symbol to q or Qval; or better, stop passing symbol names as bare strings altogether; create the Symbol explicitly with Q = symbols("Q") and pass that Symbol object to solve, solve(gf, x, Q, y), rather than the string "Q".

question:
Loading pytest fixtures from separate Poetry package

I am trying to move some test configuration into a common Poetry package to avoid repetition of the same fixtures. In a project there is a package named user-service with tests folder inside. Inside that folder I am trying to load fixtures in user-service/tests/conftest.py : import pytest from httpx import AsyncClient, ASGITransport from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession from user_service.main import app from common.core.database import get_db from common.tests.db_conf import ( # noqa: F401 anyio_backend, test_engine, setup_db, db_session, ) pytest_plugins = ["common.tests.db_conf"] # Setup http client @pytest.fixture async def client(db_session: AsyncSession): async def override_get_db(): yield db_session app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = override_get_db async with AsyncClient( transport=ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://users_test" ) as ac: yield ac app.dependency_overrides.clear() as you see, I am trying to load fixtures from common project. common/common/tests/db_conf.py : import os import pytest from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import ( AsyncSession, create_async_engine, async_sessionmaker, AsyncEngine, ) from sqlalchemy import NullPool from sqlalchemy.engine import URL from common.models.base import Model pytest_plugins = ["anyio"] @pytest.fixture(scope="session") def anyio_backend(): return "asyncio" # Setup test database engine @pytest.fixture(scope="session") def test_engine(): DATABASE_URL = URL.create( drivername="postgresql+psycopg", username=os.getenv("POSTGRES_USER"), password=os.getenv("POSTGRES_PASSWORD"), host=os.getenv("POSTGRES_HOST"), port=os
reference_answer: The issue was unrelated to the pytest plugins. I am running my tests with the docker compose and I forgot to add package folders in volumes. During every run, my code was out of date and that is why I thought that nothing helps. Full project is inside public github repo: https://github.com/Misha4231/two-phase-commit-fastapi/tree/main That line is enough to load the fixtures from separate poetry package: pytest_plugins = ["common.tests.db_conf"]
llm_attempt: Two likely culprits. First, common needs to actually be installed into user-service's virtualenv for the common.tests.db_conf import to resolve at all; a shared monorepo folder layout alone isn't enough, so add it as a path or editable dependency in user-service's pyproject.toml so it lands on site-packages. Second, and easy to miss: pytest only reliably honors a pytest_plugins = [...] declaration by dotted path when it's defined in the rootdir's top-level conftest.py; declaring it in a non-root conftest.py, like user-service/tests/conftest.py, is deprecated and restricted in modern pytest versions and can silently fail to register the plugin. Move pytest_plugins = ["common.tests.db_conf"] to the actual root conftest.py of your test run, or better, turn common.tests.db_conf into a proper installable pytest plugin using a pytest11 entry point in common's pyproject.toml instead of relying on the dotted-path pytest_plugins mechanism across separate packages, the more robust pattern for shared fixtures across packages.

reference_answer: Far too many questions in that. Issue 3 : Missing Elements in style.element_names() The set of elements is searched in a hierarchy of themes. To the vista theme inherits from xpnative which inherits from the default theme. So if you can't find something in element_names() in your current theme it is in one of the ancestor themes (probably default). The ones listed in the current theme are defined in this theme. I don't know if the introspection lets you find out the theme hierarchy but they all have 'default' as an ultimate ancestor. style.theme_use('default') style.element_names()
llm_attempt: What you're seeing is expected, if confusing: style.configure() writes into Tk's style/resource database and echoes back whatever key or value you set, including arbitrary ones like text, but that doesn't mean every element actually reads that option when rendering. For Button.label, the displayed text comes from the individual widget's own -text option or -textvariable, not from the style database; each button obviously needs different text, so the style layer intentionally doesn't drive content that way, even though element_options() lists text as a technically settable option on that element. So style.configure("TButton", text=...) gets stored and returned by a later configure() call, but has no visual effect on existing or new Button widgets; it's effectively a no-op for content. Only genuinely visual options, background, foreground, font, padding, relief, anchor, and similar, are meaningfully themable this way. To set text, use button.config(text=...) or a textvariable on each instance directly instead of trying to drive it through the style system.
